paras: The Sixth and Vine street attack was an assault by a white crowd on three Black men at Sixth and Vine streets in central Cincinnati, Ohio, early on the morning of November 24, 1903, after the men were accused of insulting two white women. A white man, John McCarthy, was stabbed three times in the melee, and the three men were "roughly handled" before police kept the crowd from killing them. The story circulated as a short wire item headed "race war" and was reprinted in Midwestern and Dakota weeklies into December 1903.

According to a Cincinnati dispatch dated November 25, two white women were standing at the corner of Sixth and Vine early in the morning when three Black men came up and, "as no one was about at that time," began to insult them. The dispatch named neither the women nor the three men and did not say what was said.

White men soon arrived, and within a few minutes a crowd had gathered and "made a rush for the negroes," while the two women got away in the melee. In the struggle John McCarthy, one of the white men, was stabbed three times, and the dispatch reported that he "may die"; it did not say who stabbed him. The three Black men were "roughly handled," and by the same account it was "only the quick work of the police" that prevented them from being killed. A shorter version of the story said simply that the men "were saved from death by the police."
No report of arrests or charges against the three men or any member of the crowd appears in the coverage, nor any later word on McCarthy's condition.

The fullest account ran in the Evening Times-Republican of Marshalltown, Iowa, on November 25 under the headline "Race War in Cincinnati" and the subhead "White Men Defend White Women from Insults of Negroes." That framing cast the crowd's rush as a defense of the women, treated the alleged insult as established, and offered no account from the three men. The same day the Minneapolis Journal compressed the story into one sentence in a column of datelined briefs, calling the clash "a riot" rather than a race war.

Weekly papers carried two condensed forms into December. The Minneapolis wording reappeared in the Northern Wisconsin Advertiser's "News of the World" on December 3. A "Crimes and Criminals" item reducing the event to a race war that had occurred "recently" ran in the Pierre Weekly Free Press and the Williston Graphic on December 3 and the Washburn Leader on December 5. The same item still appeared in the Pioneer Express and the Emmons County Record on December 11, more than two weeks after the event. No Cincinnati paper's account and no Black-press report of the episode appears in the coverage.

bases: A white crowd rushed and 'roughly handled' three Black men accused of insulting white women and was kept from killing them only by police (A1, A2, A3); no one was killed.

accounts.label: Cincinnati wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Three Black men insulted two white women at Sixth and Vine; white men gathered and rushed them; McCarthy was stabbed three times and may die; police barely prevented the Black men from being killed.

accounts.label: Condensed brief
accounts.gist: Same story in one sentence, calling the clash 'A riot' and saying the men 'were saved from death by the police'.

framing.detail: The subhead 'White Men Defend White Women from Insults of Negroes' presents the crowd's rush as defense and states the alleged insult as fact, with no version from the three men.
Briefs and weekly digests repeat the story in one sentence ('A riot ensued'; 'A race war ... occurred ... recently') without comment.
